questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t)=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sinh}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+16{sinh}^{2}⁡t{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t(1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sinh}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡4.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi {e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t/2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t,$ or $2\,\text{d}u={e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi ({e}^{t}+1)\cdot {e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}8\pi ({u}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16\pi ((\frac{8}{3}+2)-(\frac{1}{3}+1)) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{14}{3}-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{10}{3}) \\  & =\frac{160\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot |{e}^{t}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot ({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t]\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ using integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⇒ & v={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}x & =t{e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi [{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{1}-{(t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t})|}_{0}^{1}] \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}+1-0)-(e-e)+(0-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-3] \\  & =({e}^{2}+2e-6)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})=6{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(6t)}^{2}+{(6{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot |6t|\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot 6t\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}$ Then, ${t}^{2}=u-1$ and $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2t\cdot {t}^{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{2{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{2({4}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{2({4}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot [(\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})) \\  & =18\pi \cdot (\frac{62}{5}-\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{116}{15} \\  & =\frac{696\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t+\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [1,e].

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=e.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{2}{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{1}{t})=1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{t})}^{2}+{(1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}+1-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{{(1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\cdot |1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+t+\frac{2}{t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+t+\frac{2}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =2\pi [(-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}+2)-(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+0)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{2{e}^{2}}+2] \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{{e}^{2}}+4)\pi .\end{aligned}

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\pi.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{3}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9(1+t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+t.$ Then, $1+3t=3u-2$ and $\textrm{d}u = \textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3u-2)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3{u}^{3/2}-2{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{6{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{4{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{6({2}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{4({2}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{24\sqrt{2}}{5}-\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{15}+\frac{2}{15}] \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{5}(16\sqrt{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$
